iut_type: End Product (Silex Technology module, for an end customer referred to as 'P company'), HOGP Host role dependency requirement dispute
customer_question: Your post-July-2024 registration site says HOGP Host (whether Report Host or Boot Host) now also requires DIS, HIDS, and BAS (and ScPS for Report Host) profile testing. But the HOGP specification's HID Device Requirements explicitly say 'Service' is Mandatory for the Device role, while for the Host role it only says 'Service Discovery' is Mandatory — and that Discovery requirement is already covered within HOGP's own ICS. Also, checking a real published Listing (the latest iPhone 15's Bluetooth registration) shows it includes HOGP but not HIDS or DIS. Based on this, we believe HOGP Host shouldn't actually require these additional services — can you double-check?
question_variants: Is the new registration site's HOGP Host dependency requirement a genuine spec rule or a site bug?
Does real-world precedent (other companies' published Listings) support skipping DIS/HIDS/BAS for HOGP Host?
actual_issue: The customer's careful reading of the HOGP specification's exact wording (distinguishing 'Service' Mandatory for Device role versus 'Service Discovery' Mandatory for Host role), combined with real-world evidence from a major company's published Bluetooth Listing, contradicted the post-July-2024 registration site's Consistency Check requirement that HOGP Host role also support DIS, HIDS, BAS, and ScPS — creating uncertainty about whether to trust the site's current behavior or the customer's spec-based interpretation.
plain_english_explanation: Checking the prior, pre-July-2024 Launch Studio registration system confirmed that HOGP Host registrations under the old system indeed did not require DIS, HIDS, or BAS support — the old system's Test Plan for HOGP Report Host only ever listed a single ScPP item alongside the standard HOGP test items, with no separate DIS/HIDS/BAS profile support requirement at all. This matched the customer's own spec-based reading and their iPhone 15 Listing precedent. Since the new Qualification Workspace system was still undergoing bug-fix work at the time (experiencing network timeouts that prevented immediate re-verification), the most likely explanation was that the new system's stricter Consistency Check requirement for HOGP Host was an unintended bug introduced during the system migration, not an actual new spec requirement — and once the system stabilized, re-running the Consistency Check with the minimum-required HOGP Host ICS items confirmed exactly that: the Test Plan reverted to only the standard HOGP items plus a single ScPP item, with no DIS/HIDS/BAS requirement, confirming the customer's interpretation was correct all along.
consultant_answer: You're right to question this — checking the prior Launch Studio system confirmed that HOGP Host registrations never required DIS, HIDS, or BAS support; the old Test Plan only ever listed a single ScPP item alongside the standard HOGP items. This matches your spec reading and the iPhone 15 precedent. The new Qualification Workspace system was still undergoing bug-fix work, so this was very likely an unintended bug from the migration rather than an actual new requirement. We've now re-confirmed with the minimum-required HOGP Host ICS items: the Test Plan correctly reverts to just the standard HOGP items plus one ScPP item, with no DIS/HIDS/BAS requirement — your interpretation was correct.
decision_logic: When a new registration site behavior contradicts both a careful reading of the underlying specification's exact wording and verifiable real-world precedent (other companies' published Listings), treat this as a strong signal of a site bug introduced during a system migration, and re-verify once the new system stabilizes rather than assuming the new, stricter behavior is automatically correct.
final_recommendation: When a customer presents a well-reasoned challenge to a registration site's behavior, backed by both specification language analysis and real-world precedent, take the challenge seriously and re-verify against the prior system's behavior and the new system's stabilized state, rather than defaulting to trusting the newest site behavior as automatically authoritative.
risk_if_done_wrong: Accepting the new system's unverified, bugged behavior at face value would have required the customer to unnecessarily run and pay for DIS, HIDS, and BAS profile testing that wasn't actually required, based on a temporary site migration bug rather than a genuine specification requirement.
